text: Windows writes event logs automatically, on every machine, whether anyone ever looks at them or not — a running record of what the operating system, its services, and its applications did, long before anything goes wrong. Event Viewer is the built-in console for reading those logs, and it's usually the first tool a SOC analyst or sysadmin opens when a ticket says something happened on this machine and nobody yet knows what.

Three ways to open Event Viewer, all landing on the exact same console: Win+X and pick Event Viewer from the menu, Win+R and type eventvwr.msc, or through Computer Management's System Tools node. eventvwr.msc is the one worth memorizing — it works from any Run dialog, any remote session, and any script, which makes it the fastest path once you already know where you're going.

Inside the Windows Logs node, five logs exist, but three carry nearly all the day-to-day weight. Application logs events from apps and services running on the machine — a crashed program, a failed install, an app-level error. System logs events from Windows itself and its core components — a driver that failed to load, a service that wouldn't start. Security logs audit events: logons, logoffs, account changes, and anything the audit policy is configured to watch.

The Security log alone requires administrator rights to read. A standard user can browse Application or System freely, but Security stays locked down, because it's the record of who logged on, who was created, and who was added to which group — exactly the kind of account and privilege activity you don't want a non-admin able to map out. Every event's General tab shows five fields worth knowing by sight: Level, Date and Time, Source, Event ID, and Task Category.

Filter Current Log narrows a noisy Security log fast, almost always by Event ID — the single most common move once you know the ID you're hunting for. Up next: the five Security-log Event IDs every analyst should recognize on sight, starting with what a successful logon and a failed logon each look like in the log.
